title: Giant Sensitive Plant: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Giant Sensitive Plant in Rice: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Giant sensitive plant, or makahiyang lalaki, is a thorny shrub of rainfed palay. Learn to spot it and clear it safely before it sets seed.
excerpt: Giant sensitive plant is a thorny, spreading shrub that farmers call makahiyang lalaki, Aroma, kapit kabag or kipi kipi. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it, how to handle its sharp spines, and how to control it before it takes hold in your bukid.

blocks.text:
In English, this weed is called the giant sensitive plant. Its scientific name is Mimosa diplotricha, and it belongs to the Mimosaceae family, the same group as the small makahiya. In the bukid, farmers call it Aroma, kapit kabag, kipi kipi, makahiya or makahiyang lalaki. The name makahiyang lalaki sets it apart from the smaller makahiya, Mimosa pudica. Since it is a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You will see it in rainfed lowland rice fields. As a perennial shrub, it lives for years and turns woody as it matures. Seed is how it spreads. Pods form after the pink to purple flowers, and the seeds drop around the parent plant. Left alone, it builds thick, thorny tangles that are hard to walk through.

blocks.text: How to Identify Giant Sensitive Plant

Look for a spreading shrub with angled stems packed with backward pointing spines. These spines catch on clothes and skin. The leaves are feathery, with 4 to 8 pairs of side branches, and each branch holds many pairs of narrow leaflets. Like other broadleaf weeds, its leaflets have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The flowers are pink to purple, and the pods are long and narrow. Older plants become woody at the base.

items: A spreading shrub that turns woody as it gets older.
Angled stems densely covered with sharp spines that point backward and catch on clothes.
Feathery leaves with 4 to 8 pairs of side branches, each holding many narrow leaflets.
Pink to purple flowers, followed by long, narrow seed pods.
Look alike tip: the small makahiya has fewer spines, and its leaflets spread like fingers at the stalk tip.

blocks.text:
Giant sensitive plant spreads into a thick, thorny shrub. It shades the palay and takes water, fertilizer and space from the rice hills it grows over. In rainfed fields, where water is often short, that competition cuts deep.

The spines are the other big problem. They scratch and cut the hands, arms and legs of anyone who weeds, plants or harvests near it. Workers tend to avoid thorny patches, so the weed gets left behind and grows even bigger. Because it is a perennial that turns woody, old plants get harder to remove each season. Its pods also add seed to the soil every year.
How to Control Giant Sensitive Plant

items: Always wear thick gloves, long sleeves and boots when you pull or cut it, because the backward pointing spines tear skin and clothes.
Cut or uproot plants before the pink to purple flowers turn into pods, so no new seed falls into the field.
Remove plants while they are still young and soft, since the shrub turns woody and much harder to uproot as it matures.
Dig out the woody base and roots of older plants, because this perennial can grow back from what you leave in the ground.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold giant sensitive plant down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Giant Sensitive Plant Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Giant Sensitive Plant?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Giant Sensitive Plant

items.q: What is giant sensitive plant called in Tagalog?
items.a: Farmers call it Aroma, kapit kabag, kipi kipi, makahiya or makahiyang lalaki. Its scientific name is Mimosa diplotricha. Because some of these names are also used for the small makahiya, check the plant closely. This one is a bigger, spreading shrub with angled stems packed with backward pointing spines.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Put on gloves, long sleeves and boots first. Then cut or uproot young plants before they flower and set pods. Dig out the woody base of older plants, and clean the bunds too. Keep water in the field where you can. If you need a herbicide, pick one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is this weed dangerous to farmers?
items.a: Its spines are the main danger. They point backward and grip skin and clothes, so they scratch and tear when you pull away. Small wounds can get infected in a wet, muddy field, so wash and cover any cut right away. Good gloves, long sleeves and boots keep you safe while you clear it.
